title: The Little Gas Station That Welcomed Everyone
summary: Route 66 is a famous road. It once ran more than 2,000 miles from Chicago to Los Angeles. Along the way stands a small gas station in Oklahoma. It tells a big story about kindness. During the Jim Crow era, most restaurants, gas stations, and motels would not serve Black families. Families had to carry their own food and gas. They used a travel guide called the Green Book to find safe places to stop. But one place always welcomed them. The Threatt Filling Station in Luther, Oklahoma, gave people fuel, food, and a place to sleep. It was the only known Black-owned gas station on the whole road. Allen Threatt Sr. built the first station in 1915. After the wooden building burned down, he built a new one from sandstone. It looked like a small, welcoming house. The station became a place for dances, barbecues, and baseball games. But new highways took the cars away, and the station closed in the 1970s. It sat empty for years. Now Threatt's grandchildren are saving it. Visitors can now see the old gas pumps from the 1940s.
why_it_matters: This station shows how one family's kindness helped travelers when most places turned them away.
